slides.body: Five mistakes to watch for.

items: Reading an empty git diff HEAD as "the next commit changes nothing". Root cause: two differences cancelled; the working tree equals HEAD while the index differs from both.
Committing a partially staged file without testing it. Root cause: the tests ran against the working tree, and the index holds a version that never existed as a file.
Looking for s on a hunk that cannot be split. Root cause: split is offered only when unchanged lines separate the changes; touching lines are one hunk and need e.
A new file is missing from the commit although the diff "looked complete". Root cause: an untracked file has no index entry, so no diff shows it; git add -N when you create it.
Trusting an edited hunk without reading git diff --cached. Root cause: a hunk edit can stage content that exists nowhere, neither in HEAD nor in the file.

beats.text: It's the end of a debugging session. One file holds three edits: a tuning change you were trying, the bug fix you found, and a debug print you forgot to remove. The fix has to go out now, on its own, so that it can be reviewed and, if necessary, reverted on its own.
beats.tele: It's the end of a debugging session. One file holds three edits: a tuning change you were trying, the bug fix you found, and a debug print you forgot to remove. The fix has to go out now, on its own, so that it can be reviewed and, if necessary, reverted on its own.

beats.text: You can do that. Git lets you stage one of the three edits, which means marking it for the next commit, and commit it. And the commit you make will contain a version of the file that has never existed on your disk, and that nobody has ever run.
beats.tele: You can do that. Git lets you stage one of the three edits, which means marking it for the next commit, and commit it. And the commit you make will contain a version of the file that has never existed on your disk, and that nobody has ever run.

beats.text: That's the trade at the centre of this video. Partial staging gives you clean commits from a messy working tree, the folder of files you edit. The price is a snapshot in the index that was never tested. You'll learn the technique, and the check that removes the risk. And that file nobody has ever run? You'll meet it by its ID.
beats.tele: That's the trade at the centre of this video. Partial staging gives you clean commits from a messy working tree, the folder of files you edit. The price is a snapshot in the index that was never tested. You'll learn the technique, and the check that removes the risk. And that file nobody has ever run? You'll meet it by its ID.

Three topics today, all consequences of the last video's one idea: the index is a full snapshot that sits between HEAD and the working tree. The index is Git's proposal for the next commit, and HEAD is the last commit you made.

beats.text: The rule for practice: make git diff --cached the last command before git commit. It's the review of what you're about to record.

beats.text: Partial staging. In one sentence: git add -p walks through the difference between the index and the working tree one hunk at a time, and stages only the hunks you accept, so one edited file can feed several commits and leave a remainder that is never committed. It is 🟢 SAFE.

beats.text: Inside .git. One new blob and one changed index entry. A blob is the object that holds one file's content. This one is HEAD's version plus the hunks you accepted: content that has never existed as a file.

beats.text: The risk, and the check. After a partial add, three versions of the file exist. HEAD has none of your edits. The working tree has all of them, and is what you ran. The index has the accepted hunks alone, and that version has never run anywhere. Before you commit it, copy the staged snapshot out of the index and test that. git checkout-index --all --prefix=<dir>/ 🟢 SAFE writes every index entry as a file below the directory you name. The trailing slash matters.

beats.text: Editing a hunk. When changed lines touch each other, they form one hunk, and s is not offered. The answer e opens the hunk as a patch, a text of added and removed lines. Deleting a + line keeps that addition out of the index.

beats.text: Replacing the - of a removed line with a space keeps that removal out. Git then recounts the hunk header and applies the patch to the index. beats.text: Intent to add. The manual: "Record only the fact that the path will be added later. An entry for the path is placed in the index with no content".

beats.text: Why is it needed? A new file is invisible to git diff, because there's no entry to compare it with. The hunk selector reads the same comparison as git diff, so it has the same blind spot, and the same cure.

beats.text: Inside .git, the entry carries an intent-to-add flag. Index format version 2 has no room for it, so Git writes the index as version 3 while such an entry exists, and as version 2 again after the real add.

beats.text: When not to. Partial staging is the wrong tool when you can't test the result and have no CI behind you, no server that tests every commit: the commit is by construction untested. And e is the wrong tool when s would do, because an edited hunk is the one place where you can stage lines that are in neither HEAD nor your file.

beats.text: Five mistakes to watch for.
beats.tele: Five mistakes to watch for.

beats.text: Reading an empty git diff HEAD as "the next commit changes nothing". Root cause: two differences cancelled; the working tree equals HEAD while the index differs from both.
beats.tele: Reading an empty `git diff HEAD` as "the next commit changes nothing". Root cause: two differences cancelled; the working tree equals HEAD while the index differs from both.

beats.text: Committing a partially staged file without testing it. Root cause: the tests ran against the working tree, and the index holds a version that never existed as a file.
beats.tele: Committing a partially staged file without testing it. Root cause: the tests ran against the working tree, and the index holds a version that never existed as a file.

beats.text: Looking for s on a hunk that cannot be split. Root cause: split is offered only when unchanged lines separate the changes; touching lines are one hunk and need e.
beats.tele: Looking for `s` on a hunk that cannot be split. Root cause: split is offered only when unchanged lines separate the changes; touching lines are one hunk and need `e`.

beats.text: A new file is missing from the commit although the diff "looked complete". Root cause: an untracked file has no index entry, so no diff shows it; git add -N when you create it.
beats.tele: A new file is missing from the commit although the diff "looked complete". Root cause: an untracked file has no index entry, so no diff shows it; `git add -N` when you create it.

beats.text: Trusting an edited hunk without reading git diff --cached. Root cause: a hunk edit can stage content that exists nowhere, neither in HEAD nor in the file.
beats.tele: Trusting an edited hunk without reading `git diff --cached`. Root cause: a hunk edit can stage content that exists nowhere, neither in HEAD nor in the file.

beats.text: Now, out of the lab. The textbook's classic "works on my machine" commit lacks a new file. The code runs locally because the file is on disk. git diff looked complete. git commit -a skipped the file, for a reason the next video explains. And CI fails with a missing module. git add -N when you create a file puts it into every later git diff, git add -p and git commit -a.

beats.text: And the reason partial staging is worth its price: a commit that does one thing can be reviewed, reverted, cherry-picked and bisected on its own. Later parts of the course teach each of those. Debugging sessions don't produce changes in that shape. Partial staging sorts one messy working tree into such commits. CI is the backstop, and the export is the local check.

beats.text: git add -p stages chosen hunks. I split with s when there's context between changes, and edit with e when there isn't. A partially staged commit records a tree that never existed in my working tree, so I export it with git checkout-index and test that. And git add -N gives a new file an entry with no content, so that diffs and the hunk selector can see it.
